items.19: All right, the chat. Looks like we are good to go there. I'll get somebody to move the minutes. Thank you, Councillor Gough. Any opposed? They're important minutes. Not seeing any. That's approved. And we'll go right into unfinished business 5.1. Ms. LaCroy, do you want to introduce that for us? We'll be able to speak. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Lynn LaCroy, General Manager of Community Services. This report comes to this committee from the Street Activity Subcommittee as a required annual update report on the activities undertaken by the Community Support Program. The program is now in its 10th year of operation and continues to have very great success in connecting people in need to the appropriate program systems and supports. Community Support Program Supervisor Mr. Rob Garrison is in attendance to speak to this matter. Mr. Garrison, is the mic working there? Yes, it does. You can go ahead when you're ready. Okay, thank you. Good morning, City Councillors and City Administration. We thought it might be prudent, since we're completing our 10th year next month — time flies — that maybe we should just tell you a little bit about what's going on and some of the challenges that we're having out there. I'm not sure what can actually be resolved quickly, but there are some urgent needs out there that we thought we'd highlight. We regularly report to the Street Activity Subcommittee on a quarterly schedule every year, and occasionally we identify trends that are very important, we think, in the community. Occasionally, our trends and speaking up about them garners some media attention. So, I just wanted to say that since we're a street-level service that interacts with all manner of organizations, services, businesses, vulnerable people, property owners, visitors to Saskatoon, and those who frequently frequent these key districts, we think that we're in a very unique position to notice and report on the trends. Our purpose for reporting it goes with our model that we've had since 2012, which is 'Safe Streets for All'. We want everyone to be safe out there and everyone to be enjoying the downtown, Broadway, and Riversdale districts. Lately, we're noticing many organizations and businesses taking measures to increase their security. For example, cameras, security staff, locking doors during business hours, reducing their services, and removing options for people to sit and visit both inside and outside their businesses. It's not just businesses I'm talking about; it's all the buildings and services downtown. These individual efforts are not without significant cost, and as things invariably work in society, the costs get passed on to the public and the services get reduced, and we're seeing that. Our response to problems that occur in areas where service providers are concentrated is that we regularly observe and interact with businesses and property owners who struggle to find solutions. Sadly, we sometimes watch a business close or move elsewhere as they tire of putting up with repeated issues, some of which are criminal occurrences. Since time is limited, I thought I'd stick to one general theme which is causing us a lot of concern, and that is the lack of shelter bed availability. In particular, for our purposes and for all the people that I mentioned that frequent downtown, it's the emergency bed shelter concern. Many people may find it interesting that despite the opening of 70-plus beds downtown this winter, we are regularly unable to secure emergency beds for people who are struggling with addictions, mental health, and/or homelessness. This is the case whether the cold weather strategy is enacted or not, and it continues every day, even now. The answer from shelters almost 100% of the time last year or this year, including in very severe weather, is, 'We're full'. It doesn't matter what time of the day or what time of the week; the answer is the same: 'We're full'. We had a difficult winter this winter with housing people under short-term circumstances. On too many occasions, we had to make multiple phone calls, and there's a lack of dignity for people when you're trying to find them their basic needs. We believe that more could be done in the area of coordinating housing. There are a lot of resources that come into Saskatoon from all different funding sources related to housing, and we don't feel that it's coordinated enough. We feel that it's not transparent enough, and that the organizations that are getting funding in order to provide housing need to work closer with organizations, with us, to ensure that there are emergency beds out there so that we can take the pressure off the streets. When one or two people are causing multiple concerns for people downtown, on any given day, we need to get them off the streets and to a safe place to detox. Thank you. Perfect timing. I'll just keep you at the mic there for a second to see if we have any questions, first of all, from in committee. I see we have Councillor Gough. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you, Mr. Garrison, for reporting on this. I found this report very helpful. In particular, the data around new individuals that your outreach services are encountering, which made me think a little bit more deeply about how you're collecting data and the granularity of that data. It's probably more granular than I had realized. So, my question to you is: has there been any discussion between the CSOs and SHIP regarding incorporating your touch points and data gathered from them into the coordinated access system that is being developed in the City of Saskatoon? We haven't had any recent contact regarding coordinated access, but as you know, we work very closely with SHIP. SHIP has its challenges as well. This winter, they tried as much as they could to help us with the issue that I was describing with emergency beds, however, and in the cold weather strategy in particular, but they struggle as well because they don't have any authority or any means to question a shelter when they say they're full and what they are doing in order to get beds freed up so that we can. So, I see them as a lot in the same boat as us. I think there should be more transparency with the people who have these beds and are having them filled all day long. If there were an opportunity to have CSO data part of the coordinated access system — and the reason I ask is because it is intended to understand where the pressure points are, not only on the way into shelter, but as you say, on the way out of shelter, and what lack of availability or coordination is there. Would your team have the capacity to... I don't know how you collect data in your daily work... would you have the capacity to access a digital terminal where you could put a computer or device, where you could access a secure network and input data into the coordinated access system if that invitation were received? In short, yes, we've been looking forward to the implementation of coordinated access for in excess of five years now. It started once and then it fizzled, and that's part of my concern with the housing: it seems like nobody has a good handle on it. I'm not saying we need more funds; I'm saying we need more coordination and perhaps to be more centralized for housing, which I think coordinated access would do. But yes, we have capacity to fully contribute to that system. I think that this report I highlighted, I sent to Council this year. It's the first time that our highest number of calls has been directed towards outreach, which is mainly homelessness, so we're spending a lot more time on the streets trying to help people with housing. We don't think that was ever intended to be our role; it takes hours and hours and follow up over days to get people effectively housed. We see our role as identifying the needs and getting them to the people who can look after housing, but certainly we can contribute. If we had coordinated access for those we meet on the street, we all have phones. We have a very good system where we could go in and check on what happened with that person yesterday or this morning, who is dealing with them, so that we can save time and get to the next call, hopefully resulting in better outcomes for individuals. Speaking of getting to calls, I'm just wondering if you could speak a little more about the response time. I was pretty impressed to see that you've maintained an average, I think it was six minutes, response time. I'm sure that average is a fairly broad figure, but I'm wondering if you can tell me just a little bit more about that, contextualize that data a little bit for me. Yes, we keep track of when we get a call, when we get to the call, when we complete the call, and the police do as well. They're on the radio with us all the time; we confirm with them every single call that we go on. So, we have a good system for tracking the times, not only the response time but how much time we're on a call. What we did notice this year is the time on a call increased, and it all goes to the stats that we keep. It makes sense because we're dealing with longer-term or more intensive problems than simply trying to get somebody to a safe place. It's more that you have to get them to some kind of a longer-term housing situation, which is very difficult, but we're proud of the response time. Every business that we deal with, and most of the service providers, are amazed and happy. Not every call is 6.5 minutes, but spread out over the year, it may take us a little longer, of course, to get up to the Rexall drugstore on Avenue O, but it all evens out. We added our bike team a couple of years ago; that didn't really change our response time, but it changed the level of visibility for uniform officers out there, which helps to deter negative activity. Great, thank you very much for adding some context and very much for the report and your additional commentary here today. Thank you. Next, we have Councillor Block. Thank you, Chair Davies, and thank you, Mr. Gerson, for speaking to this today. I'm interested to better understand; you said over and over again you hear there's no room. Can you tell me if there are beds available? Why is there no room? Do you have any insight into that? I'm really trying to better understand if it's also that there aren't enough beds, or is it simply the coordination? And where do you think that falls through in your mind? Well, we think that a certain amount of it is due to a lack of coordination. For example, three or four years ago, we had a good system for somebody who needed detox, even if the bed was spoken for that day or that night. We asked them, and some of them readily did it; they would change the sheets and make that bed available for three, four, five hours while the person detoxes so that we could get that pressure off the streets. Businesses rely on us to try to get a person a ways away from their doorway or away from the issues they're causing so that they can just have a little bit of a break sometimes during the day. It's a lot of pressure that's being put on businesses and others in our small communities downtown, Broadway, and Riversdale, but we think that the beds could be used better. COVID, I guess, had a little bit to do with it. I'm not buying that at all. I think the beds could be used more efficiently. There's one shelter that gives people until nine o'clock that night to report, and if they don't report, then that bed is made available. I say that all the people who are honestly looking for shelter that night are already looked after or have made their decisions by nine o'clock at night. We hope so for a lot of the people that we deal with. We're trying to get them in the shelter at six o'clock, five o'clock, seven o'clock in the evening so that they're safely tucked away. We don't want people, especially vulnerable women, out there looking for shelter at nine o'clock and maybe being turned away. Then what? Because we can't find them a bed, so where are they going to find a bed? I'm hearing you say that there might be a bit of a process issue: if the shelters are tabulating one person, one bed per day, you would run into difficulty if the need is potentially for a few hours here and there, and then overnight. Is that what I'm hearing you say? Yes, I think there could be a lot more coordination that way to maximize the efficiency. Of course, those are expensive beds, we all know. I feel that the organizations could be working closer with us if we tell them that the need is there to get this person off the street. We don't want the police to have to arrest; that's a whole different situation that kicks in. It's not a good reason just to say somebody's intoxicated and they have to be arrested when we could be doing better ourselves with the beds that are funded. So, I'm just going to wrap here. We're getting a little bit into the weeds here on the annual report side of things, so I'm trying to guide us back to the report there, if we could. Those are my questions for the speaker. I would have some questions for our administration at the appropriate time. Thank you very much, Mr. Gerson. I'm not seeing any other questions for Mr. Gerson. Thanks for coming here with us today. We have some further questions for administration. Councillor Block, you're free to go first. Thank you, Chair Davies, and I apologize if this is going in the weeds with regards to the annual report, but it certainly has been part and parcel of our conversations amongst our council colleagues in recent weeks. It's top of mind for businesses in the downtown and for many residents of downtown, which I represent. I'm wondering if our administration can provide any further insight on this, and how does this problem and potential solution move forward with regards to all the other data and information that we've been gathering over the last number of weeks? Thank you, Mr. Chair. Through you to Lynn LaCroy, General Manager, Community Services. On a number of occasions, we have had some conversations about our upcoming contract with SHIP. We also are going to be providing an information report in the not too distant future, I believe at perhaps the next PDCS, possibly the May Council meeting, just on the housing continuum, where and how the city fits in, and how there can be an interrelation or perhaps a better coordination of programs and services. Some of this will be our forward-looking approach to the community-wide Community Safety and Well-being Framework and who has parts to play in each of those. And then also some work that will be underway in the formalization of our Renewed Housing Business Plan that we will be embarking on, gathering more information and data throughout the year to again develop a more coordinated approach across the continuum within the community. So, those are some reports that you will have forthcoming; those are some initiatives related to housing, directly and indirectly, that will be coming forward at future meetings. I appreciate that, Ms. LaCroy. Through the Chair, just one quick follow-up: will part of that plan... Require a partnership in some regard with the province. Through you Mr. Chair to the Councillor, absolutely the province is embedded in the conversations in housing, in particular in the area of social housing, where that is their primary mandate for the provision of programs and services. There are definitely conversations with the province along the way whenever conversations about housing and homelessness come up. Thank you very much. Those are my questions. Any other questions for administration before we move on to comments? Not seeing any comments. I'm just going to check virtually. Councillor Gough: Thanks, Mr. Chair. I just want to first say a thank you to Mr. Grayson and his team for the really incredible work that they do in our community and all of the work done to make efforts to coordinate among services and also identify pressures that are being faced. And having gone to see the work up a little bit more closely in some of the earlier stages of the pandemic, I can attest to a very collaborative attitude with respect to trying to assist folks who are requiring assistance in our downtown and core business areas. I think that the trends that we're seeing in this report reinforce the trends we've been speaking about in these chambers over a number of meetings and that we've been hearing from the sector. I think that, well, I know that Mr. Harrison is absolutely correct that there is a tremendous amount of pressure at the intake end of the sheltering, emergency sheltering, and of the continuum. There's also tremendous pressure at the outflow end of the emergency sheltering services and of the continuum. And a huge amount of what we understand from the sector relating to why that is, is because there is not appropriate support of housing for people facing addictions issues in our community; that is the core of it. And there aren't the health services to go along with that or the support of services for that housing. What we see is folks being transitioned to housing and coming back through the emergency sheltering system, or there's simply nowhere appropriate to transition folks to, when we saw that in the STC data. We would hear it from any of the service providers, and so I think service providers are facing a real challenge when it comes to figuring out how much of their staff resources to put into continually flipping beds versus trying to do the work to try to get somebody more stably housed in community. And there's no right answer, and so I feel very encouraged knowing that the function of coordinated access is coming, but I feel especially encouraged that we have such dedicated folks with 10 years of experience on our streets doing this work every day, because the reality is they care deeply and we are not the only community facing these challenges. Seeing the number of new folks that the CSO program interacted with over the last year: 131 new people. It's a tremendous issue that we're facing in our community, and it is going to take the whole sector and all orders of government to tackle it. So I'm really looking forward to the housing continuum report. I'm really looking forward to more conversations about the world of ship and how the city is supporting that work. And just want to thank everybody involved in trying to figure this out because there is no one simple answer, but we certainly have a lot of the pieces in place, and the dedication among the folks who are working, I think, across that continuum is untold. So, thanks. And are you willing to move those recommendations be received? Thank you. Any other comments? Not seeing any, so that's been moved by Councillor Gough. Any opposed? And that carries. 5.5 Recovery Park Public Art Scope Change. Thank you, Mr. Chair. This report is to inform the committee that administration has adjusted the scope of the public art project plan for the new waste diversion facility, known as Recovery Park. Recovery Park is a facility separated from the landfill where the public can deposit materials not intended for the landfill, thus improving recycling options for residents. The public art component of the project was identified as part of the overall scope of the project in the June 2021 report to EUCS on the overall budget for Recovery Park. This public art plan is consistent with the intentions identified within the Public Art Policy. The public art is meant to enhance the design of the facility while at the same time serving as a communication or education tool regarding the importance of recycling and environmental sustainability. With the scope change, instead of a single artwork at Recovery Park, there will now be three artworks. One will be located at Recovery Park itself, while two others will be in different locations in the city. These locations will be determined by administration and consultation with the successful artists and stakeholders. Having three artworks at three locations will enhance the awareness of Recovery Park and broaden the city's efforts in communicating the importance of environmental sustainability. There's no financial implication to this scope change. The RFQ remains at $275,000 plus $35,000 in contingency. The funds are for consultants to design, fabricate, and install three works of art. A number of administration staff are available if there are any questions on this report.

First for questions, we have Councillor Loewen. Thank you, Mr. Chair. My question, I think, has more to do with the future application of policy, and I'm supportive of this direction in this specific situation. But what I'm wondering is, in the future, if there's an interest in distributing the allocation in different locations beyond the location from which the capital contribution is originating, what is the trigger for that? I think this is where the committee could have asked about it earlier because we did approve it at the committee level before there was a call for submissions. But in the future, if there's a capital contribution from a project, what's the process for flagging whether or not the art is going to be at that same location, in multiple locations, or in a completely different location? I'm just not clear on, next time we have a similar situation, what our process is going to look like and what the responsibility of the committee is to direct that, if any.

Mr. Chair, if I may, Mr. Kevin Kitchen, Manager of Community Development, is here and available to answer any questions. Thank you very much, Councillor.

Kevin Kitchen, Community Development Manager: Great question. The answer to that is, it's really a discussion, a negotiation between the Public Art Program and the client department that is hosting the capital project. The way the policy is written, there's no absolute requirement that there has to be public art anywhere. It's where it makes sense, where there's value, where it aligns with the capital project itself. A bit of background: for Recovery Park, it wasn't so much the policy or the program seeking out Recovery Park for public art. It was more the other way around, where it was identified that public art could enhance the communication and the work that they were doing at Recovery Park. I think, in answer to your question, that's something we can trigger. We can ask those questions earlier. I think, in hindsight, we've come to a better conclusion this time around. With the support of the host department, there is an interest in seeing the artwork spread out over the city. So, I think that's something that we will take back and make sure that we ask when we have those initial negotiations or discussions with the host department.

Okay, I know we're very early in the life of this program, so we're just going to have to learn as we go. Great, thank you very much. And that's been moved by Councillor Gough. So I'll call the question in the opposed. And that carries 5.7, the temporary pause of civic naming program.
Mr. Gray: Yes, thank you, Mr. Chair. Committee will recall that Council funded the legacy review project through the 2022-23 budget process. This will develop a phased strategy to addressing naming recognition and other aspects to recognize and celebrate the histories, cultures, and identities of Indigenous peoples and other diverse communities in Saskatoon. Through this project, we expect there will be changes to both the policy and program administration associated with civic naming. Continuing to administer the program under the current approach may not align with the future goals of the program and will require administrative time and effort that could otherwise be used to further the legacy. The application and use of names from the names list occurs when a name for a new street, park, or civic facility is required. Between 2016 and 2021, 150 names were added to the list, including 68 resulting from the 'Name the North Commuter Parkway Bridge' initiative. While over that same period, only 48 names were required for streets, parks, and civic facilities. On average, we need eight to 12 names per year, and as of the writing of this report, there are currently 125 names on the names master list. Administration is proposing to pause the receipt and review of new naming submissions at this time until the legacy review has been brought forward and perhaps a new or amended policy addressing civic naming. The pause will allow staff to focus on efforts involved in the legacy review and the renaming of John A. Macdonald. There is one recommendation in the report, and administration is available if there are any questions.
